$comment: Seed label space for the UK-first v1 model. 60 species: the original 57 plus Lepiota brunneoincarnata, Amanita pantherina and Cortinarius orellanus, added to close the coverage gaps named in docs/REVIEW.md. gbif_key is resolved at prepare time by scripts/resolve_gbif_keys.py -- deliberately null here rather than guessed. Toxicity and diagnostic characters are drawn from standard UK references (Kibby, Phillips, Buczacki) and MUST be reviewed by a qualified mycologist before any public release. See docs/SAFETY.md.
$policy: The `toxicity` field records a KNOWN HAZARD and is used only to drive warnings. It is never rendered as a recommendation. This app makes no edibility claim of any kind: there is no value meaning edible and none meaning inedible. `NO_RECORDED_TOXICITY` says the references used recorded no toxicity -- a statement about records, not about a meal -- and it is never shown to a user. The `notes` field is shown to users verbatim and must describe only what is observable. Rationale, policy and review flags belong in `internal_note`, which is never surfaced.
$character_states: character_states is complete -- every species carries states for the characters it declares as diagnostic -- and is UNREVIEWED throughout. It was derived from each species' own `notes` in this file rather than from a mycologist, to make the answer-weighting mechanism in server/app/evidence.py work end to end. Complete is not reviewed: every entry still needs field-character sign-off, reviewed_by is null and /health reports taxonomy_reviewed: false. How wide a state list should be depends on the species' role, and the difference follows from the risk matrix. For a DEADLY species a contradiction pushes it down, so lists are generous -- omitting a state it can show would turn a true observation into a false dismissal of something lethal. For the safe half of a lethal pair a contradiction pushes the SAFE species down, moving mass back toward the deadly one, so tighter lists are the cautious choice and the cost of error is a false alarm rather than a missed poisoning. Where the notes make no positive claim the entry is omitted, because omitted means 'no evidence' and is always safe. See docs/REVIEW.md and docs/character-states-worksheet.csv.

species.notes: Aniseed smell and a pendulous cog-wheel ring. The critical checks are absence of a volva and absence of chrome-yellow staining at the stem base.
species.internal_note: Carries no toxicity record, by the same policy as agaricus-campestris.

species.notes: Gills pink when young, darkening to chocolate-brown. Brown spore print. No volva at the stem base and no chrome-yellow staining when cut.
species.internal_note: No toxicity recorded. This app asserts neither edibility nor inedibility for any species; the field records hazards only. See docs/SAFETY.md.

species.notes: Fibrous brown-scaled cap in conifer woods, the flesh reddening strongly when cut. Chocolate print, ring, and no volva.

The commonest cause of mushroom poisoning in the UK. The stem base stains chrome yellow when cut, and the smell is phenolic or of ink. Both reactions are strongest at the very base of the stem, which is why the whole fruit body must be collected.

bruising_reaction: Yellow, especially at the stem base

species.notes: Pale lemon to almost white, with a rounded basal bulb that has a distinct rim rather than a loose sac. Smells strongly of raw potato, which the Death Cap does not. Not itself dangerous, but it is the species most often taken for a Death Cap and the one most often used to argue that a Death Cap is harmless.
species.internal_note: No toxicity recorded, which is not the same as harmless: this sits inside Amanita, where the cost of a confident mistake is fatal.

species.notes: Grey-brown cap with grey, easily washed-off patches, a grooved ring, and a basal bulb without a free sac. Sits between the Blusher and the Panther Cap in appearance: it does not redden like the first and does not have the sharp collar of the second.
species.internal_note: Added because the app carried both species it is confused with and not the thing between them, so a photograph of it was forced into one of the two.

species.notes: Tawny-orange cap with a strongly grooved margin, no ring at all, and a tall white sac at the base. Toxic raw. The missing ring is what separates it from the deadly Amanitas, and an absent character is a poor thing to hang a decision on.
species.internal_note: TOXIC by the same policy as Amanita rubescens: toxic raw, and the margin for error sits inside Amanita.

species.notes: Pale yellow cap with white patches and a fragile ring that frequently disappears. Shares the ibotenic acid and muscimol of the Panther Cap, which it hybridises and intergrades with.

Ibotenic acid and muscimol; deliriant rather than lethal, but hospitalisation is common. Included in the label space because it is the most photographed fungus in the world and the model must handle it confidently.

Ibotenic acid and muscimol at higher concentration than the Fly Agaric, and hospitalisation is the usual outcome. Brown cap with pure white warts, a white ring, and a distinct collar-like rim at the top of the basal bulb. The flesh does not redden when cut, which is the separation from the Blusher.
species.internal_note: Added per docs/REVIEW.md item 11. Classified SERIOUS rather than DEADLY: deaths are recorded but rare, and the usual course is severe intoxication. It sits in Amanita, so the dangerous-genus rules apply regardless of this classification.

species.notes: Responsible for the majority of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. Free white gills, white spore print, membranous ring, and a sac-like volva at the stem base which is often buried and missed. Olive-green to yellowish cap. Ectomycorrhizal, usually with oak or beech.
Flesh reddens where damaged or grub-eaten, which is the character the common name refers to. Toxic raw.
species.internal_note: Widely treated as edible when thoroughly cooked. Classified TOXIC here because it is toxic raw and because the margin for error sits inside Amanita, where a misidentification is potentially fatal. Do not relax this without mycological review.

species.notes: Grey cap with a strongly grooved margin, rising from a white sac at the stem base. It has a volva and no ring, which is the combination that separates it from the death cap and the destroying angel -- both of those carry a ring as well. Toxic raw.
species.internal_note: Added because a beginner taught 'a volva means danger' meets this and is wrong, and a beginner who has not been taught it meets this and reads it as a destroying angel. Common (FRDBI rank 244) in a genus holding three DEADLY or SERIOUS species already in the label space. Widely eaten cooked; classified TOXIC for the same reason as Amanita rubescens and Amanita fulva -- toxic raw, and the margin for error sits inside Amanita. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Entirely white, including the gills, which stay white at all ages. White spore print. Ragged ring and a sac-like volva. Young buttons are readily mistaken for puffballs; sectioning vertically reveals the developing cap and gills.
Grey-brown cap over cream decurrent gills, on a stem swollen into a club at the base. Causes a severe reaction with alcohol.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Clitocybe clavipes.

species.notes: Pear-shaped puffballs in dense crowds on rotten wood, joined at the base by white cords. The only puffball that grows on wood in numbers. The inside is white when young and olive-brown once it matures.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Lycoperdon pyriforme.

species.notes: White to cream spore print, which separates it from the rust-brown Galerina. Toxic raw and upsetting to some people even cooked.
Gelatinous purple blobs and discs crowded on dead beech, often merging into a brain-like mass.
Small pale yellow to ivory bonnet in grass and conifer litter.
Gelatinous ear-shaped bracket, overwhelmingly on elder.
Thin grey-brown tiered brackets whose pore surface is smoky grey, almost black at the edge — the feature that names it.
Egg-yellow slimy cap that flattens, fades to grey and collapses within a day, on dung-enriched grass.
White pores ageing yellow-olive, a pale raised network on the upper stem, and flesh that does not blue. Any boletes with red pores are excluded by the safety layer.

stipe_surface: Netted or with a raised mesh

species.notes: Rubbery black-topped discs like buttons, crowded on fallen oak bark, brown and felty underneath. Sheds black spore dust over whatever touches it.
White papery crust peeling away from fallen branches, the surface wrinkled into a shallow net.
Tiny unbranched yellow spines scattered in numbers along dead broadleaf wood.
Pale yellow spoon-shaped stagshorn, mostly on conifer wood. A recent arrival in Britain that has spread quickly.
Bright orange-yellow antler-shaped branches, tough and rubbery rather than brittle, rooting into buried conifer wood.
Strong mealy smell of fresh bread dough, white spore print, spring fruiting. Shares its season with the deadly Inocybe erubescens.
Very large and effectively unmistakable at full size, but the same white-interior check applies.
Blunt forking false gills running down the stem, not true blade-like gills. Apricot smell. Flesh white throughout when torn.
Large fan-shaped bracket with flattened brown scales in concentric rows, on standing and fallen hardwood in spring. Smells of watermelon rind.
species.internal_note: Also published as Polyporus squamosus, which is the name the First Nature index uses. Recorded under the current combination; flagged in REVIEW.md. Also confused with polyporus tuberaster, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Small cinnamon bolete with rusty-orange pores and bright yellow flesh in the stem base. Fiercely peppery. Usually near fly agaric.
The blue-green stain in fallen wood is seen far more often than the tiny turquoise cups that produce it.
Causes gastric upset in a substantial minority of people even when cooked. Smooth stem without snakeskin patterning, abrupt basal bulb, flesh reddening when cut.
Coarsely shaggy cap on a smooth stem, the flesh turning saffron then red-brown when cut. Separating it from Chlorophyllum brunneum needs the stem base, and neither should be taken on a photograph.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Macrolepiota rhacodes.

species.notes: Bright purple smooth underside on small wavy brackets; the fungus that causes silver leaf in plums and cherries.
Ash-grey branched coral in woodland litter. Much of what is recorded as this is the crested coral overtaken by mould.
White coral whose branches end in fine crests and points, in woodland litter. Often greyed by a parasitic mould.
Thick white clubs, wrinkled and grooved lengthwise, barely branched.
Apricot-yellow coral branching into antler tips, in unimproved grassland.
Unbranched bright yellow spindles in tufts in short grass, brittle rather than rubbery — which is what separates a club from a stagshorn.
Taxonomically entangled with Clitocybe rivulosa and treated as equivalently dangerous. Crowded decurrent gills in short grassland.

Small pale funnel smelling strongly of aniseed. It is a small white Clitocybe, and the muscarine species are small white Clitocybes; the smell is the only easy separation and smell is not a safe basis.
Grey-brown, drying two-toned from the centre outwards, in leaf litter under broadleaves. The deadly ivory funnels are white and grow in grass.
species.internal_note: Usually listed as inedible or suspect rather than poisonous. Classified TOXIC because it sits in the group that contains the muscarine species already in the label space, and because the cheaper error here is a false warning. A reviewer may downgrade. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Large, grey and cloud-capped, in troops and rings in leaf litter. Strong mealy smell. Upsets a substantial minority of people even when cooked, and shares its habitat and season with the dangerous Entoloma sinuatum.

High muscarine content; fatalities are rare but recorded. Decurrent gills running down the stem, versus the free-to-adnexed gills of Marasmius oreades. Shares the same short grassland and lawn habitat, and often the same fairy rings.
Small, grey-brown, funnel-shaped, with a strong smell of raw meal. In leaf litter and moss under broadleaves and conifers.
species.internal_note: Same reasoning as Clitocybe metachroa: suspect rather than documented, classified TOXIC because of the company it keeps. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Strongly decurrent gills and a pink spore print. The decurrent gills are the separation from the dangerous Entoloma sinuatum, whose gills are sinuate.
Crowded tufts in leaf litter, the caps fading to buff and the thin stems finely downy and fused at the base.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Gymnopus confluens.

species.notes: Tan cap on a stem thickly woolly at the base, binding leaf litter together. Peppery.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Gymnopus peronatus.

species.notes: Tiny wrinkled white caps on fallen twigs, especially bramble.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Gymnopus ramealis.

species.notes: Hundreds of tiny pleated buff caps swarming over a stump at once, greying and collapsing within a day.
Tawny, finely grooved caps dusted with mica-like flecks when fresh, in dense clusters on and around stumps. The gills darken and the cap dissolves into ink. No ring.
species.internal_note: Shares stumps and clustered habit with Galerina marginata. The black print and the deliquescence are what separate them.

species.notes: Contains coprine, which causes a severe disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol consumed within several days. Grey-brown smooth cap without shaggy scales.
Silvery-furry cylinder opening into a ragged grey parasol and gone by afternoon, on woodchip and litter.
Tall shaggy cylindrical cap that dissolves into black ink from the margin upwards.
A cobwebby veil across the young gills and a rust-brown spore print place it in Cortinarius. Greyish to lilac-brown, with ochre bands on the stem.
species.internal_note: The label space held only the two orellanine webcaps and Cortinarius violaceus, so every common webcap a user photographed had nowhere accurate for its mass to go. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Contains orellanine, with the same delayed kidney failure as the Deadly Webcap: onset two to three weeks after the meal, long after anyone connects the illness to the mushroom. Broadleaf woodland, particularly oak, where Cortinarius rubellus is with conifers. Implicated in mass poisonings following confusion with chanterelles.
species.internal_note: Added per docs/REVIEW.md item 12: only C. rubellus was present, leaving the other orellanine-containing webcap outside the label space.

species.notes: Contains orellanine. Kidney failure onset is delayed by 2-3 weeks, so victims rarely connect the illness to the meal. Rusty-brown spore print, cobwebby cortina on the stem, true gills. Conifer woodland, often among Sphagnum.

Deep violet throughout with a scaly cap and rusty spore print. Present in the label space so the model learns the Cortinarius/Lepista boundary, which matters because the genus contains deadly members.
Hollow funnel, smooth to slightly wrinkled outer surface, no true gills.
As the variable oysterling and separable from it only under a microscope; recorded distinctly, photographed identically.
Small, with a brown spore print, separating it from the white-spored oyster mushrooms it grows alongside.
Tiny white kidney-shaped brackets on the underside of fallen twigs, the gills turning pinkish-brown.
Apricot-buff, dry, faintly felty cap with thick waxy gills running well down the stem. Unimproved grassland.
species.internal_note: Safe half of a lethal pair; tight lists. Older references call it Hygrocybe pratensis.

species.notes: Pure white, slightly greasy cap with thick waxy gills running down the stem, in unimproved grassland. White spore print. It shares its ground with the deadly white Clitocybes, and the waxy decurrent gills are what separate them.
species.internal_note: The safe half of a lethal pair, so its character lists are kept tight: a contradiction here pushes mass back toward the Clitocybes. Older references call it Hygrocybe virginea.

species.notes: Small ochre cap covered in a granular mealy powder, with a ragged ring zone and an earthy smell. Mossy ground.
species.internal_note: Points at the small Lepiota species: a granular scaly cap with a ring is exactly the impression the deadly small dapperlings give.

species.notes: Tiny orange-yellow gelatinous blobs scattered in numbers over wet dead conifer wood and fence posts.
Flat semicircular bracket on willow and birch, its pores elongated into slots or maze-like plates, bruising red-brown where rubbed.
Hard black hemispheres on dead ash and beech, showing concentric silver-and-black rings when cut through. Woody rather than fleshy, and present all year.
species.internal_note: Also confused with kretzschmaria deusta, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Dark brown crust with a narrow bracket edge, the pore surface stretched into a coarse maze.
Silky brown conical cap in grassland with gills turning clear pink. The genus holds Entoloma sinuatum, and a pink print in grass is worth taking seriously.
Greyish-brown, in damp broadleaf woodland, with a smell of raw meal. Pink spore print. Slimmer and more fragile than the livid pinkgill.
species.internal_note: SERIOUS, decided by Martin Hawkes 2026-09-23. Raised from TOXIC: a significant cause of poisoning where it is eaten, and flagged here as an open review question alongside Entoloma sinuatum, which was already SERIOUS. Toxicity grading overall still awaits mycological sign-off.

species.notes: Small and white to cream, in damp grassland, the gills flushing pink with age. A white mushroom whose pink spore print is the thing that places it.
species.internal_note: Small white grassland mushroom, which is the shape of several things that matter. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Dark brown, silky when dry, in short grass, smelling strongly of raw meal or radish. Gills turn pink as the spores mature.
species.internal_note: Common in exactly the lawns and churchyards where people pick fairy ring champignons. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: A leading cause of mushroom poisoning in Europe. Pink spore print and pink-flushing gills at maturity. Separated from The Miller by gill attachment: sinuate/adnexed here, strongly decurrent in Clitopilus prunulus.
Black gelatinous lobes with a warted surface, swelling along dead oak branches after rain and shrivelling to a thin crust in dry weather.
Translucent colourless jelly lumps on fallen broadleaf wood, each holding opaque white grains visible against the light.
White to translucent folded jelly cushions on dead attached beech branches.
Marbled red flesh exuding red juice, on oak and sweet chestnut.

Tawny slimy caps in tufts on elm and other broadleaf stumps in the depth of winter, on a stem that turns black and velvety from the base. Galerina marginata fruits in the same weather on the same wood; the white spore print is the check.
Grey hoof-shaped bracket, hard as wood, banded in concentric ridges, high on birch and beech trunks. Perennial, so the same bracket is there year after year.
species.internal_note: Also confused with ganoderma applanatum, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Smooth pale kidney-shaped bracket, only ever on birch. Rubbery when young and corky when old, with a white pore surface.
species.internal_note: Also published as Piptoporus betulinus, the name used by the First Nature index. Recorded under the current combination; flagged in REVIEW.md. Also confused with ganoderma applanatum, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Rust-brown flat porecrust with very fine pores, spread over dead broadleaf branches.
Tiny, tawny, scattered among moss rather than clustered on wood, and without a ring. The funeral bell is larger, grows in clusters on dead wood and carries a ring.
species.internal_note: Galerina marginata was the genus's only member, so any small tawny Galerina was a funeral bell as far as the label space was concerned. Classified TOXIC rather than left without a toxicity record because amatoxin content across this genus is not uniformly established and the cost of under-warning inside Galerina is death. A reviewer should confirm. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Contains the same amatoxins as the Death Cap. Grows in clusters on dead wood, which is exactly where foragers look for Sheathed Woodtuft. Rust-brown spore print. The distinction from Kuehneromyces mutabilis is genuinely difficult and is the single most dangerous confusion for experienced foragers.
Massive hard perennial bracket at the base of living broadleaf trees, the white pore surface bruising brown at a touch and shedding cocoa-brown spore dust over everything beneath it.
As the southern bracket but thinner-fleshed, with a crust you can draw on by bruising it. Separating the two reliably needs a section.
Dull grey-brown waxcap under a thick layer of slime, with white gills.
Very slimy pinkish-orange waxcap of acid grassland and heath, the gills decurrent with a gelatinous edge.
Slimy cap, green at first and fading through yellow to pink, in unimproved grassland. The green slime is unmistakable while it is fresh.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Hygrocybe psittacina.

species.notes: Orange-tawny cap, rusty spore print, very bitter. On conifer wood, in groups rather than tight tufts. Any ring is at most a faint zone.
species.internal_note: Rusty print and conifer wood put it in the same frame as Galerina marginata, which is the reason it is here.

species.notes: Minute brown parachutes on black horsehair stems, binding conifer needles and dead leaves with black runners.
Tan to russet cap, crowded pale gills, and a tough hollow stem that springs back rather than snapping. In leaf litter, often in troops.
Tough tufts at the foot of oak, on grooved spindle-shaped stems twisted together and rooting. Gills spot rusty.

Contains gyromitrin, which metabolises to monomethylhydrazine. The cap is irregularly brain-like or saddle-shaped, not regularly pitted like a true morel, and the interior is chambered rather than a single hollow cavity. Spring, usually with conifers.
Pallid clay cap, greasy when damp, smelling strongly of radish, with gills that weep droplets in wet weather. A plain mushroom in exactly the places beginners look.
Ivory saddle-shaped cap folded over a deeply ribbed and pocketed hollow stem, on woodland paths and verges.
species.internal_note: TOXIC: contains hydrazine compounds of the same family as Gyromitra. Graded conservatively; please confirm.

species.notes: Lumpy brown bracket with a white rim and white pores, low down on conifer stumps and roots.
Spines rather than gills or pores on the underside. Among the most distinctive genera in the label space and a useful sanity check on model calibration.
Small waxy yellow cap with gills running a little down a dry stem.
Bright lemon-yellow slimy cap and a slimy yellow stem, in unimproved grassland. Does not blacken.
Blood-scarlet cap and stem, the gills scarlet with a yellow edge. Does not blacken with age.
Scarlet to orange sharply conical cap that blackens all over with age or handling. Grassland. Reports of poisoning exist.
species.internal_note: TOXIC on the conservative reading of a contested record; please confirm.

species.notes: Tiny orange-red waxcap with a greasy stem yellow at the top and orange below.
The largest scarlet waxcap, with a fibrous streaked stem white at the base. An indicator of old undisturbed grassland.
Dull orange waxcap with a distinct oily smell, sometimes likened to bedbugs or to Lactarius quietus.
Orange-red waxcap smelling of honey, strongest as it dries.
True gills, thin, crowded and repeatedly forking; orange flesh rather than white. Upsets some people.
Rigid dark rust-brown brackets curling off oak stumps, the underside smooth and velvety.
Slimy wrinkled cap on a long stem with a deep tapering root down to buried wood. The root is what names it and what identifies it.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Xerula radicata.

species.notes: Very common on stumps and dead wood. Greenish-yellow gills darkening to purple-brown, and an intensely bitter taste. Its clustered habit on wood mirrors that of the woodland species foragers commonly collect.
Salmon-pink hemispherical cushions crowding dead beech branches, darkening to brick and then black.
Small hard purple-brown cushions scattered over dead hazel and alder branches.
Bay-brown cap, slightly greasy when wet, cream to yellow pores that bruise blue-green. The stem is brown-streaked but never netted.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Boletus badius.

species.notes: Large buff funnel with a small central boss, in long arcs and rings on woodland edges.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Clitocybe geotropa.

species.notes: Pale tan funnel with crowded white gills running down a slender stem, in leaf litter.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Clitocybe gibba.

species.notes: Severe muscarine poisoning; fatalities recorded. Radially fibrous cap staining red where handled or bruised. Appears in spring alongside St George's Mushroom, with which it has been fatally confused.
Small, silky-white, sharply conical cap with a distinct central point, and a strong earthy smell. The gills age to dull clay-brown and the spore print is brown. Contains muscarine.
species.internal_note: SERIOUS rather than TOXIC: muscarine poisoning is rarely fatal but is a hospital matter. Lists are generous because a contradiction pushes it down, and this is not a species to dismiss lightly.

species.notes: The lilac form of the white fibrecap: same silky pointed cap, same earthy smell, same muscarine. Mistaken for the amethyst deceiver, which prints white where this prints brown.
species.internal_note: Long treated as Inocybe geophylla var. lilacina. SERIOUS for the same reason, with the same generous state lists.

species.notes: Crusty pinkish-brown cushions merging into sheets along dead birch branches, black and pimpled with age.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Annulohypoxylon multiforme.

species.notes: Flat grey-white crust at first, then a brittle black sheet that looks like burnt paint at the base of beech. A serious structural rot.

Scaly stem below the ring and a two-toned hygrophanous cap. The app will not return this at species level when Galerina marginata is in the candidate set, because the two cannot be reliably separated from photographs.
Deep violet throughout when fresh, fading to buff as it dries, which is where the name comes from. Thick, widely spaced gills and a white spore print.
species.internal_note: Also confused with mycena pura, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Tawny to brick-pink and fading as it dries, which is what the common name refers to. Thick, well-spaced, flesh-pink gills and a white spore print. The stem is fibrous and twisted. Its variability is the hazard: it looks like a great many other things, and beginners match a great many other things to it.
species.internal_note: No toxicity recorded, by the same policy as the rest. Added for frequency (15,266 FRDBI records) and because it is the commonest false anchor a beginner reaches for.

species.notes: Shaggy tawny cap with very dark mottled gills that weep dark droplets, leaving a black-speckled ring zone on the stem. Paths and verges.
Slimy grey-green cap with faint darker spots in concentric rings, always with beech. Acrid white milk drying grey.
Exudes carrot-orange latex that slowly stains green. Pine woodland.
Small greyish-lilac milkcap smelling strongly of desiccated coconut, with birch.
Grey-buff cap with well-spaced ochre gills, under hazel. Ferociously acrid milk.
Dull red-brown cap with faint concentric banding, white milk, and a distinctive oily smell. Always with oak.
Brick-red funnel with a small central point, under conifers. The acrid taste builds slowly and then burns.
Red-brown milkcap of beech woods with copious white milk and a mild taste that turns slightly bitter.
Small orange-brown milkcap whose white milk stains a handkerchief yellow. With birch.
White acrid latex and a shaggy inrolled cap margin. With birch.
Dark olive-brown, almost black cap with a woolly inrolled edge, with birch. White milk, very acrid.
Widely eaten but causes reactions in a significant minority, and specimens from yew, eucalyptus or conifers are regarded as unsafe. Host tree matters, so the app asks for it.
Dark scabrous scales on a pale stem; strictly with birch.
Slimy olive-and-ochre club with a rolled, irregular head, in damp litter.

Contains the same amatoxins as the Death Cap. Small, with a pale cap broken into pinkish-brown concentric scales and a fragile ring that is often gone. Fruits in grass -- lawns, parks, roadside verges -- where nobody expects a lethal mushroom, and has caused repeated fatal poisonings in Europe among people gathering small field mushrooms.
species.internal_note: Added because docs/REVIEW.md item 10 named the small brown Lepiota species as the most significant gap in the label space: amatoxin-containing, present in the UK, and absent from the taxonomy. A species the model has never seen cannot be flagged, and would be forced into the nearest class it knows -- here, a lawn mushroom.

species.notes: Small, with a white cap bearing concentric reddish-brown scales and a dark central disc. Smells unpleasantly of rubber or burnt hair. Very common in gardens, verges and woodland paths.
species.internal_note: Included mainly as a reference class for the small Lepiota group: it is the one people actually meet, and without it the lethal members have no common sibling to be distinguished from.

species.notes: Contains the same amatoxins as the Death Cap. Small, with a pinkish-brown scaly cap on a paler ground and a fragile ring that is often gone by the time it is found. Grass, verges and garden borders, alongside the small lawn mushrooms people pick.
species.internal_note: Added alongside L. brunneoincarnata: carrying one lethal small Lepiota and not its sibling is arbitrary, and the two are not separable in the field by a non-expert.

species.notes: Toxic raw and must be thoroughly cooked. Pale pinkish-buff spore print, no cortina, distinguishing it from purple Cortinarius species.
Tall pestle-shaped puffball on a long stalk that persists through the winter as a hollow cup.
Dark brown puffball covered in blackish spines that leave a net of scars when they fall. Heath and conifer litter.
Interior uniformly pure white and homogeneous when young. Any trace of gill structure means an Amanita button; any darkening means an earthball or an over-mature specimen.
Snakeskin-patterned stem and a double ring that slides freely. Flesh does not redden strongly, separating it from Chlorophyllum.
Widely spaced free gills, a tough pliable stem, and a broad umbo. Shares lawns and fairy rings with the deadly Clitocybe species, which have crowded decurrent gills.
White pleated parachute on a black wiry stem, the gills attached to a collar that stands free of the stem. On twigs and rootlets.
Broad streaky grey cap with very wide white gills, attached to buried wood by thick white cords.
Huge rosette of overlapping fan-shaped fronds at the foot of beech, the whole thing blackening where bruised.
Regularly pitted honeycomb cap, fully hollow from cap tip to stem base when sectioned lengthways, and the cap fused to the stem along its length.
Translucent white caps under a thick layer of slime, high on dead beech branches, with a ring on the stem.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Oudemansiella mucida.

species.notes: Olive-grey to yellowish bonnet on dead broadleaf wood, smelling strongly of iodine as it dries.
Greasy grey cap on a yellow, sticky stem; the whole cap skin peels away as an elastic film.
Slender grey bonnet on a thread-like stem, smelling of iodine when drying.

Grey-brown bell-shaped cap with a low central point, white spore print, and gills joined by cross-veins. Tufted on stumps. The white print is the check that matters: the deadly Galerina on the same stump prints rust brown.
Small grey bonnet whose stem bleeds white milk when snapped. Leaf litter.
Wine-red bonnet in small tufts on dead wood, bleeding dark red-brown juice from the stem when broken.

Dense tufts on oak stumps, the stem yellowing then rusting from the base, with a mealy or faintly chemical smell. The white spore print is what separates the whole clustered-bonnet habit from the deadly Galerina.
Grey bonnet with a strong smell of bleach or ammonia, in litter and moss.
Grey bell-shaped cap on a rigid, silvery stem finely grooved along its length, rooting into buried wood.
Lilac to pink cap, a strong radish smell, white spore print, on leaf litter. Contains muscarine.
Rose-pink cap, radish smell, in beech litter. Contains muscarine, as does Mycena pura, which it was long treated as a form of.
Tiny red-brown bonnet in litter and moss, bleeding dark red from the stem and edged red along the gills.
Minute white bonnet frosted all over with tiny hairs, on fallen twigs.
Small grey-brown bonnet on a long wiry stem that snaps with an audible click, rooting into buried twigs.
Red-orange pores and flesh that turns deep blue within seconds of cutting. Toxic raw. The stem is covered in fine red dots rather than the raised net of the Devil's Bolete.
species.internal_note: Also confused with suillellus luridus, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Red-pored bolete blueing instantly where cut, the stem covered in red dots rather than a net. Any bolete with red pores is excluded by the safety layer.
species.internal_note: Long treated as a form of Neoboletus luridiformis.

species.notes: Sharp-edged true gills running down the stem, orange throughout, clustered on buried roots and stumps. Severe gastrointestinal poisoning. The gills are the separation from the Chanterelle, which has blunt forking ridges rather than blades.
True sharp-edged gills and a clustered habit on wood or buried roots. Severe gastrointestinal poisoning. Rare in the UK but present in southern Europe and North America.
The commonest lawn mushroom in Britain, drying out from dark brown to buff in bands. Mottled dark gills.
species.internal_note: TOXIC as a conservative grading for a small brown lawn mushroom that is routinely picked by children and is easily confused with several others.

species.notes: Slim conical dark brown cap on a long stem, in manured grass.
Grey bell cap hung with white veil fragments round the rim, on dung and rich pasture. Black mottled gills.
Small tan kidney-shaped brackets in tiers on oak stumps, with crowded gills and a fiercely astringent taste. Faintly luminous in the dark.
Tawny-orange funnel with crowded gills running well down the stem, in troops and rings in conifer and broadleaf litter.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Lepista flaccida.

species.notes: A pleated grey parasol the size of a fingernail that opens at dawn on lawns and has collapsed by midday.

Causes a cumulative immune-mediated haemolytic syndrome that can be fatal and may develop only after years of apparently safe consumption. Strongly inrolled cap margin; gills bruise reddish-brown. Formerly eaten after cooking in parts of Europe; now regarded as unsafe in all preparations.
Lilac-grey waxy crust on fallen oak twigs, curling away from the bark at the edges when dry.
Found by smell long before sight: a carrion stench that draws flies to the olive slime on the cap. Emerges from a white egg in leaf litter and woodchip.
species.internal_note: Also confused with mutinus caninus, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Orange to violet-pink waxy crust on dead broadleaf wood, radially wrinkled with a paler fringed edge.
Soft gelatinous white-to-orange sheets with a folded, veined underside, peeling back into small brackets.
Tiny whitish bonnet on fallen twigs and bark, the gills running a little down the stem.
Dry upturned scales on cap and stem; clustered at the base of living trees.
Thin, pure white, ear-shaped and stemless, on conifer wood. Long eaten, then linked to a cluster of fatal encephalopathy cases, chiefly in people with impaired kidney function.
species.internal_note: Recorded SERIOUS rather than DEADLY: the deaths are documented but concentrated in a susceptible group. The classification is a judgement call and is flagged in REVIEW.md.

species.notes: Decurrent gills running onto an off-centre or absent stem, white to lilac spore print, on hardwood.
Free gills that start white and turn clear pink, a pink spore print, and neither a ring nor a volva. On dead wood, often buried wood, which makes it look as though it is growing from soil.
species.internal_note: The pink free gills are shared with young Amanita and with Entoloma; the combination that settles it is a pink print with no volva.

species.notes: Grey-green shield on wet willow and alder wood, the stem base bruising blue-green. Free pink gills and a pink print, as the deer shield has.
Smooth tan cap on a short stem that is jet black at the base, on fallen broadleaf branches.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Polyporus varius.

species.notes: Small soft white bracket on conifer wood that stains blue-grey where handled or with age.
Pale honey cap fading to near white, fringed with veil scraps, in clusters over buried wood on verges and lawns. Very fragile.
Very fragile tall-stemmed brittlestem, the gills edged pink-red, in litter and among nettles.
Dense tufts of date-brown caps drying to buff, on broadleaf stumps. Shares its stump with the funeral bell; the dark purple-brown print and the absence of a ring are the separation.

Straw to tan conical cap splitting radially from the rim inwards, with a brown spore print and an earthy smell. One of the more dangerous muscarine fibrecaps, and it fruits on woodland paths and verges where people look.
species.internal_note: Long known as Inocybe rimosa, and reference books still use that name. SERIOUS for the same reason as the rest of the muscarine fibrecaps; state lists are generous accordingly.

species.notes: Sharply conical cap with a distinct nipple and a separable gelatinous skin, in unimproved grassland. Bruises blue-green at the stem base.
species.internal_note: Possession and picking are controlled in the UK. It is here because it is common and because the small brown mushrooms it is confused with include Galerina marginata.

species.notes: A greasy, butter-feeling cap fading from dark red-brown, on a stem swollen and rooting at the base. Conifer litter.
species.internal_note: Older references call it Collybia butyracea.

species.notes: White cap and stem freckling all over with rust-red spots, crowded gills, bitter. Conifer litter and heath.
Pinhead orange cap on a thread stem, always among moss, with gills running far down the stem.
Red pores, blueing flesh, and a red-flushed netted stem. Violent gastrointestinal poisoning, especially raw. Chalk woodland in southern England.

stipe_surface: Netted or with a raised mesh

species.notes: Dark purple-red cap, often almost black at the centre, with white brittle gills. Under oak and beech.
Very pale pink-white fragile brittlegill of wet birch ground; the cap skin peels almost to the centre. Hot.

Flexible greasy gills that do not shatter, and brittle chalk-like stem flesh. Green-capped Russula species have been fatally confused with the Death Cap; absence of volva and ring is the decisive check.
Acrid, burning taste. Cap cuticle peels readily. Conifer woodland and Sphagnum.

cap_cuticle: Peels easily, most of the way

species.notes: Uniformly honey-straw cap, gills and stem, smelling of stewed apple or geranium. Beech. Very hot.
Small, very brittle purple-and-olive mottled cap with a finely toothed gill edge. Hot.
Very widely spaced thick gills, and flesh that reddens and then blackens where cut. Whitish at first, going sooty all over. The dead cap often persists on the ground for weeks.
Scarlet cap, white gills and stem, acrid and burning to taste. Under beech, where the Sickener proper is with conifers.
One of the commonest British fungi; included so the model has a well-populated ochre-capped reference class.
Dull wine-buff cap whose skin falls short of the rim, leaving a pale band of gills showing at the edge. Mild.
A scarlet cup on mossy fallen hardwood, through the winter and into spring when almost nothing else is fruiting.
species.internal_note: Also confused with aleuria aurantia, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: White to cream crust spread flat over the underside of dead branches, the pores torn into irregular teeth and slots.
Sectioned vertically, the interior is firm and purple-black from an early stage, whereas a true puffball is uniformly pure white throughout. The outer skin is thick and warty.
Brown scurfy earthball on a distinct stalk, the inside solid purple-black from early on. Thin-skinned for an earthball, which makes the cut the check that matters: a puffball is pure white inside.
Tiny scarlet discs on wet rotten wood, rimmed with stiff black hairs like eyelashes.
Cream lobed brain-like mass at the base of conifers.
Bleeds red like S. rugosum but forms wavy bracket edges and is on oak.
Bright yellow-orange hairy brackets and crusts fused in tiers along dead branches. The underside is smooth -- no pores -- which is what separates it from the turkeytail.
Thick pale crust on dead hazel and birch that bleeds red when scratched while fresh.
Half-sphere of pale yellow slime on a long slender stem, straight out of dung. Dark mottled gills.
Dull buff-pink greasy cap with wide compound olive pores and no ring, under pine.
No ring, and young pores exude milky droplets.
Glossy golden slimy cap with yellow pores and a ring on the stem, always under larch.
Glutinous cap and a distinct purple-banded ring. Pine woodland.
Thick white bracket, often greened by algae, with pores stretched into radial slots. Beech stumps.

Thin, flexible, banded in concentric zones of every colour from cream to near-black, in overlapping tiers on dead hardwood. The underside is finely pored, which separates it from the crusts it grows beside.
species.internal_note: Also confused with stereum hirsutum, trametes gibbosa, which are outside the label space. Recorded here rather than in `lookalikes` because that graph must only reference species the model can actually name; they are candidates if the label space grows.

species.notes: Bright yellow-orange gelatinous folded lobes on dead attached branches, shrinking to a hard crust in dry weather and reviving when it rains.
Small thin brackets in ranks along fallen conifer logs, violet on the pore surface while fresh.
Long eaten in Europe, then linked to fatal rhabdomyolysis after repeated large meals. Now legally restricted in some countries. Yellow gills and flesh; sandy pine woodland.
Slimy red-brown streaked cap with yellow gills that spot rusty, and yellow flesh in the stem. Always with birch.

Grey cap broken into darker fibrous scales, white gills and a stout white stem. Causes violent and prolonged gastrointestinal poisoning and is a leading cause of mushroom poisoning in parts of Europe. Calcareous woodland, often with beech.
Smells of household soap, and the flesh in the stem base turns pink or reddish when cut. Colour is unreliable -- grey, olive, brownish or nearly white on different collections.
species.internal_note: Carried partly because its variability is the point: a user matching on colour alone will match it to almost anything, including the tiger knight. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Sulphur-yellow throughout and smelling strongly of coal gas or tar, which no other yellow knight does. Under broadleaves.
species.internal_note: The smell is the whole identification and is unmistakable in the field; it is also the reason this is worth carrying, because the yellow Tricholoma a user is afraid of is T. equestre. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Grey, dry and felted or finely fibrous, under pine. Smaller and more slender than the tiger knight, whose cap is spotted with distinct dark scales on a paler ground.
species.internal_note: SERIOUS, decided by Martin Hawkes 2026-09-23. Raised from TOXIC: this was flagged here as an open review question, because T. terreum has been implicated in rhabdomyolysis in the same literature that made T. equestre SERIOUS. The evidence is thinner than for T. equestre and the call was made deliberately in the safer direction. Toxicity grading overall still awaits mycological sign-off.

species.notes: Chestnut to date-brown, slimy when damp, under beech. The gills and flesh stain reddish-brown where bruised.
species.internal_note: Contains ustalic acid. UNREVIEWED: compiled from standard references for this repository, not from a mycologist.

species.notes: Yellow cap densely covered in purple-red woolly scales, with bright yellow gills, on conifer stumps.
Small tan cap fringed with white veil scurf, on woodchip and buried twigs through the winter. Rust-brown print, as the funeral bell has.
Pores flushing pink with age and a dark coarse network on the stem. Overwhelmingly bitter; harmless but ruins a dish.

stipe_surface: Netted or with a raised mesh

species.notes: Cap attached to the stem only at the very apex and hanging free like a thimble, unlike a true morel whose cap is fused along its length. Causes loss of muscular coordination in some people.
Has a volva but no ring, and a pink spore print. Included specifically because it is the classic trap for anyone taught that a volva alone identifies an Amanita.
Waxy greyish crust that develops under the bark of dead attached oak branches and rolls it back as it grows.
Brown cap that cracks into a network showing red flesh in the fissures. Yellow pores, bruising faintly blue.
Dry suede-textured olive-brown cap with wide bright yellow pores and a ribbed stem.

stipe_surface: Netted or with a raised mesh

species.notes: Thread-thin black-and-white candlesnuff growing only from buried beech mast husks.
Small black antler-shaped or flattened stalks, white and powdery at the tips when young, on dead stumps all year round.
Swollen black club-shaped fingers in small groups from buried wood and stumps, white inside.
Chalk-white flat crust painted over living elder bark, cracking as it dries. Unmistakable on its host and hard to place off it.
